questions.question: A relation is in 1NF when which condition holds?

options.A: Each attribute contains atomic values in the chosen relational model
options.B: Every non-key attribute depends on the whole key

questions.answer_text: Each attribute contains atomic values in the chosen relational model
questions.description: 1NF requires each cell to contain an atomic value relative to the chosen domain and model.

questions.question: What is the central condition for 2NF?

options.A: It is in 1NF and each non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key
options.B: It has no transitive dependency only
options.C: Every determinant is a candidate key

questions.answer_text: It is in 1NF and each non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key
questions.description: 2NF removes partial dependency of non-prime attributes on a proper subset of a candidate key.

questions.question: What is the usual condition for 3NF, stated via functional dependencies?

options.A: For every nontrivial X→A, X is a superkey or A is prime
options.B: Every determinant must be a superkey

questions.answer_text: For every nontrivial X→A, X is a superkey or A is prime
questions.description: This is the formal 3NF condition; it permits some dependencies whose RHS is prime.

questions.question: What is the defining BCNF condition?

options.A: For every nontrivial FD X→Y, X is a superkey
options.C: Every relation has a single-column key

questions.answer_text: For every nontrivial FD X→Y, X is a superkey
questions.description: BCNF requires every nontrivial determinant to be a superkey.

questions.question: How do BCNF and 3NF compare in general?

options.A: BCNF is stricter; every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not conversely

questions.answer_text: BCNF is stricter; every BCNF relation is in 3NF, but not conversely
questions.description: BCNF strengthens the determinant condition, so some 3NF relations fail BCNF.

questions.question: A partial dependency is possible only when which key situation applies?

options.A: A candidate key is composite
options.B: Every key is a single attribute

questions.answer_text: A candidate key is composite
questions.description: A partial dependency is dependence on a proper subset of a composite candidate key.

questions.question: A transitive dependency commonly describes which pattern?

options.A: Key→non-key and non-key→another non-key attribute
options.B: A key depending on a foreign key only

questions.answer_text: Key→non-key and non-key→another non-key attribute
questions.description: A non-key attribute depending transitively on a key through another non-key attribute is the classic 3NF anomaly.

questions.question: What is a prime attribute?

options.A: An attribute that appears in at least one candidate key
options.B: An attribute that is always numeric

questions.answer_text: An attribute that appears in at least one candidate key
questions.description: Prime attributes belong to some candidate key, not necessarily only the selected primary key.

questions.question: What does a lossless-join decomposition guarantee?

options.A: Joining decomposed relations reconstructs exactly the original relation without spurious tuples

questions.answer_text: Joining decomposed relations reconstructs exactly the original relation without spurious tuples
questions.description: Losslessness means decomposition does not introduce extra tuples and preserves the original information.

questions.question: What does dependency preservation mean?

options.A: Functional dependencies can be enforced on decomposed relations without joining them
options.B: All original rows are stored in one table

questions.answer_text: Functional dependencies can be enforced on decomposed relations without joining them
questions.description: Dependency preservation allows checking the original dependencies using projected dependencies on individual decomposed relations.

questions.question: Can a BCNF decomposition fail to preserve all functional dependencies?

options.A: Yes
options.C: Only if there are no keys

questions.answer_text: Yes
questions.description: BCNF decomposition can sacrifice dependency preservation, unlike a 3NF synthesis that can preserve dependencies.

questions.question: What is a common goal of 3NF synthesis?

options.A: Lossless decomposition that preserves dependencies

questions.answer_text: Lossless decomposition that preserves dependencies
questions.description: A standard 3NF synthesis algorithm aims to preserve dependencies and achieve losslessness.

questions.question: What is a multivalued dependency X→→Y associated with?

options.A: Independent sets of Y values for a given X, motivating 4NF

questions.answer_text: Independent sets of Y values for a given X, motivating 4NF
questions.description: Multivalued dependencies represent independent multi-valued facts and can cause redundancy addressed by 4NF.

questions.question: What is the defining 4NF condition?

options.A: For every nontrivial MVD X→→Y, X is a superkey
options.B: Every FD determinant is a candidate key only

questions.answer_text: For every nontrivial MVD X→→Y, X is a superkey
questions.description: 4NF extends key-based normalization to nontrivial multivalued dependencies.

questions.question: What is a modification anomaly?

options.A: Updating one fact in multiple rows can leave inconsistent copies
options.B: A query uses too many indexes

questions.answer_text: Updating one fact in multiple rows can leave inconsistent copies
questions.description: Redundantly storing the same fact creates risk of inconsistent updates.

questions.question: What is an insertion anomaly?

options.A: A fact cannot be inserted without an unrelated fact or placeholder
options.B: A row is inserted twice by a trigger only

questions.answer_text: A fact cannot be inserted without an unrelated fact or placeholder
questions.description: Poorly decomposed relations can force unrelated data to be present before one fact can be recorded.

questions.question: What is a deletion anomaly?

options.A: Deleting a row unintentionally removes the only record of another fact

questions.answer_text: Deleting a row unintentionally removes the only record of another fact
questions.description: When multiple facts are coupled in one relation, deleting one fact may erase another fact’s only representation.

questions.question: What is a functional dependency X→Y?

options.A: Rows agreeing on X must agree on Y
options.C: X and Y are foreign keys
options.D: X must be a primary key

questions.answer_text: Rows agreeing on X must agree on Y
questions.description: A functional dependency constrains tuples: equal X values imply equal Y values.

questions.question: What is the attribute closure X+ under a set of FDs?

options.A: All attributes functionally determined by X

questions.answer_text: All attributes functionally determined by X
questions.description: Closure is computed by repeatedly applying FDs whose determinants are already in the current set.

questions.question: How can X be tested as a superkey using closure?

options.A: If X+ contains every relation attribute
options.C: If X appears on every RHS
options.D: If X is a foreign key

questions.answer_text: If X+ contains every relation attribute
questions.description: X is a superkey exactly when its closure contains all attributes of the relation.

questions.question: What makes a superkey a candidate key?

options.A: Minimality: no proper subset is itself a superkey
options.C: It is chosen by the DBA

questions.answer_text: Minimality: no proper subset is itself a superkey
questions.description: A candidate key is a minimal superkey; removing any attribute must lose uniqueness.

questions.question: What does Armstrong’s augmentation rule state?

options.A: If X→Y, then XZ→YZ
options.C: If X→Y and Y→Z, then Z→X

questions.answer_text: If X→Y, then XZ→YZ
questions.description: Augmentation allows adding the same attribute set to both sides of a valid FD.

questions.question: What does Armstrong’s transitivity rule state?

options.A: If X→Y and Y→Z, then X→Z
options.D: If X→Y, then X→Z for all Z

questions.answer_text: If X→Y and Y→Z, then X→Z
questions.description: Transitivity derives X→Z when X determines Y and Y determines Z.

questions.question: What does the reflexivity rule state?

options.A: If Y is a subset of X, then X→Y
options.D: If X is a key, it determines no attributes

questions.answer_text: If Y is a subset of X, then X→Y
questions.description: Reflexivity gives trivial dependencies from a set to any subset of itself.

questions.question: What is a trivial functional dependency X→Y?

options.A: Y is a subset of X
options.B: X is a subset of Y only

questions.answer_text: Y is a subset of X
questions.description: An FD is trivial when the right-hand side is contained in the left-hand side.

questions.answer_text: An equivalent set with single-attribute RHSs and no extraneous attributes or redundant dependencies
questions.description: A minimal cover is an equivalent irredundant FD representation, usually with singleton right sides.

questions.question: What does an extraneous attribute in an FD mean?

options.A: An attribute can be removed from a determinant or RHS without changing the closure implications
options.D: A table has a composite key

questions.answer_text: An attribute can be removed from a determinant or RHS without changing the closure implications

options.A: 3NF under the formal FD condition

questions.answer_text: 3NF under the formal FD condition
questions.description: With all attributes prime, the RHS-prime alternative satisfies the formal 3NF test for every nontrivial FD.

options.A: Yes, because no proper nonempty subset of that key exists

questions.answer_text: Yes, because no proper nonempty subset of that key exists

ACID Properties, Database Instance and Schema

questions.question: What does `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` commonly request in supporting DBMSs?

options.A: Lock selected rows for update

questions.answer_text: Lock selected rows for update
questions.description: FOR UPDATE requests row locks for rows selected, with behavior and availability varying by DBMS.

questions.question: What does a schema describe?

options.A: The logical structure of database objects and relationships

questions.answer_text: The logical structure of database objects and relationships
questions.description: A schema is the organization/definition of database structures, distinct from the current instance data.

questions.question: What is a database instance?

options.A: The data stored at a particular moment

questions.answer_text: The data stored at a particular moment
questions.description: An instance is the current database state at a point in time.

questions.question: What is a database transaction?

options.A: A logical unit of work consisting of one or more operations

questions.answer_text: A logical unit of work consisting of one or more operations
questions.description: A transaction groups operations for atomicity and consistency under DBMS transaction rules.

questions.question: Which ACID property means a transaction is all-or-nothing?

options.A: Atomicity

questions.answer_text: Atomicity
questions.description: Atomicity ensures the transaction’s operations commit as a unit or are rolled back.

questions.question: Which ACID property requires valid constraints before and after a committed transaction?

options.A: Consistency

questions.answer_text: Consistency
questions.description: Consistency requires transactions to preserve declared database invariants.

questions.question: Which ACID property concerns concurrent transactions appearing appropriately separated?

options.A: Isolation

questions.answer_text: Isolation
questions.description: Isolation controls how concurrent transactions interact and what intermediate effects are visible.

questions.question: Which ACID property means committed changes survive failures?

options.A: Durability

questions.answer_text: Durability
questions.description: Durability ensures committed results survive crashes according to the DBMS recovery guarantees.

questions.question: What is a dirty read?

options.A: Reading data written by another transaction that has not committed
options.B: Reading a row twice after commit

questions.answer_text: Reading data written by another transaction that has not committed
questions.description: A dirty read exposes uncommitted changes that may later be rolled back.

questions.question: What is a non-repeatable read?

options.A: Re-reading a row and seeing a committed value changed by another transaction
options.C: Reading duplicate rows in one query

questions.answer_text: Re-reading a row and seeing a committed value changed by another transaction
questions.description: A concurrent committed update can make the same row return different values on repeated reads.

questions.question: What is a phantom read?

options.A: A repeated predicate query sees added/removed qualifying rows
options.B: A row changes its value only
options.C: A query reads uncommitted data only

questions.answer_text: A repeated predicate query sees added/removed qualifying rows
questions.description: A concurrent transaction can insert or delete rows matching a range predicate between executions.

questions.question: Which isolation level is the weakest in the SQL standard?

options.A: READ UNCOMMITTED

questions.answer_text: READ UNCOMMITTED
questions.description: READ UNCOMMITTED permits the broadest visibility of uncommitted changes among standard levels.

questions.question: Which standard isolation level aims for behavior equivalent to serial execution?

options.A: SERIALIZABLE

questions.answer_text: SERIALIZABLE
questions.description: Serializable isolation is intended to produce an outcome equivalent to some serial order of transactions.

questions.question: Does `READ COMMITTED` generally prevent dirty reads?

options.A: Yes

questions.answer_text: Yes
questions.description: READ COMMITTED prevents reading uncommitted data, though non-repeatable and phantom reads may still occur.

questions.question: What is a lost update?

options.A: One transaction overwrites another transaction’s update without incorporating it
options.C: A committed row is deleted by cascade
options.D: A query loses its ORDER BY

questions.answer_text: One transaction overwrites another transaction’s update without incorporating it
questions.description: A lost update occurs when concurrent read-modify-write operations overwrite each other’s result.

questions.question: What is a deadlock?

options.A: Transactions wait cyclically for resources held by one another
options.B: A table has no primary key

questions.answer_text: Transactions wait cyclically for resources held by one another
questions.description: A cycle in the wait-for graph can prevent all participating transactions from proceeding.

questions.question: How can a DBMS typically resolve a detected deadlock?

options.A: Abort one victim transaction to break the cycle

questions.answer_text: Abort one victim transaction to break the cycle
questions.description: Aborting a selected transaction releases its locks so others can proceed.

questions.question: What does two-phase locking (2PL) generally require?

options.A: A growing phase acquiring locks followed by a shrinking phase releasing locks
options.D: One shared lock per table only

questions.answer_text: A growing phase acquiring locks followed by a shrinking phase releasing locks
questions.description: 2PL prohibits acquiring new locks after a transaction begins releasing locks.

questions.question: What is strict 2PL’s useful property?

options.A: Exclusive locks are held until commit/abort, aiding recoverability

questions.answer_text: Exclusive locks are held until commit/abort, aiding recoverability
questions.description: Strict two-phase locking holds write locks to the end, preventing cascading rollback in common models.

questions.question: What is a shared lock generally used for?

options.A: Reading while allowing other compatible readers
options.B: Writing while blocking all readers only

questions.answer_text: Reading while allowing other compatible readers
questions.description: Shared locks usually permit concurrent reads but conflict with exclusive write locks.

questions.question: What is an exclusive lock generally used for?

options.A: Writing while excluding conflicting readers/writers

questions.answer_text: Writing while excluding conflicting readers/writers
questions.description: An exclusive lock protects modifications against conflicting accesses.

questions.question: What does MVCC stand for?

options.A: Multi-Version Concurrency Control

questions.answer_text: Multi-Version Concurrency Control
questions.description: MVCC uses multiple row versions/snapshots to support concurrency, with details varying by DBMS.

questions.question: What is a common benefit of MVCC?

options.A: Readers can often see a consistent snapshot with less reader-writer blocking
options.D: It guarantees serializable behavior at every isolation level

questions.answer_text: Readers can often see a consistent snapshot with less reader-writer blocking
questions.description: MVCC can let reads use snapshots rather than blocking on writers, though isolation specifics vary.

questions.question: What does a B-tree index primarily support efficiently?

options.A: Equality and range searches on ordered keys

questions.answer_text: Equality and range searches on ordered keys
questions.description: Balanced tree indexes maintain ordered keys and support point/range lookups and ordered traversal.

questions.question: What does a hash index typically support best?

options.A: Equality lookup
options.B: Range scan in sorted key order

questions.answer_text: Equality lookup
questions.description: Hash indexes are designed for equality search and generally do not provide ordered range traversal.

questions.question: What is a composite index on (a,b) primarily ordered by?

options.A: a first, then b within equal a values

questions.answer_text: a first, then b within equal a values
questions.description: A conventional composite B-tree is lexicographically ordered by its leading key columns.

questions.question: For index (a,b,c), which predicate most directly uses the leftmost prefix?

options.A: a = 5 AND b = 7

questions.answer_text: a = 5 AND b = 7
questions.description: The leading columns of a composite index are usually most directly usable for seeks.

questions.question: What is the leftmost-prefix principle?

options.A: Leading columns of a composite index usually determine efficient index access
options.B: The first column must be a primary key
options.C: Indexes can only contain one column
options.D: The leftmost table is always scanned first

questions.answer_text: Leading columns of a composite index usually determine efficient index access
questions.description: Queries using a leading prefix can often seek into a composite B-tree, while gaps may limit use.

questions.question: What is a covering index for a query?

options.A: An index containing all columns needed to filter and return the query result
options.B: An index on every table in the database
options.D: An index that prevents table scans forever

questions.answer_text: An index containing all columns needed to filter and return the query result
questions.description: A covering index can satisfy query access from index data alone, subject to engine design and visibility checks.

questions.question: What is a clustered index in systems that use that concept?

options.A: An index whose organization is tied to the physical/logical row storage order
options.B: An index with no leaf nodes
options.D: An index that is always non-unique

questions.answer_text: An index whose organization is tied to the physical/logical row storage order
questions.description: Clustered storage associates table row organization with an index key, with exact implementation varying by DBMS.

questions.question: What is a nonclustered/secondary index?

options.A: A separate access structure pointing to table rows or primary keys

questions.answer_text: A separate access structure pointing to table rows or primary keys
questions.description: Secondary indexes provide alternate lookup paths and refer to underlying row storage.

questions.question: What is index selectivity?

options.A: How narrowly a predicate filters rows, often related to distinctness

questions.answer_text: How narrowly a predicate filters rows, often related to distinctness
questions.description: Highly selective predicates match a small fraction of rows and may make index access attractive.

questions.question: Why might a DBMS choose a table scan despite an available index?

options.A: The query returns a large fraction of rows or scan cost is estimated lower
options.B: Indexes cannot be used for reads
options.C: The table has a primary key

questions.answer_text: The query returns a large fraction of rows or scan cost is estimated lower
questions.description: The optimizer compares estimated costs; sequential scanning can be cheaper for low-selectivity queries.

questions.question: What is an index maintenance cost?

options.A: Inserts, updates and deletes must also maintain the index
options.D: Index maintenance occurs only at startup

questions.answer_text: Inserts, updates and deletes must also maintain the index
questions.description: Every additional index consumes storage and adds work to data modifications.

questions.question: Can indexing every column improve overall performance?

options.A: No; excessive indexes increase storage and write overhead
options.D: No index can help any query

questions.answer_text: No; excessive indexes increase storage and write overhead
questions.description: Indexes can speed selected reads but incur maintenance, storage, and optimizer complexity costs.

questions.question: What does `EXPLAIN` commonly show?

options.A: The query execution plan or estimated plan

questions.answer_text: The query execution plan or estimated plan
questions.description: EXPLAIN reports how the optimizer expects to execute a query; analyze/actual modes vary by DBMS.

questions.question: What does a cost-based optimizer use when choosing a plan?

options.A: Statistics and estimated costs of candidate operations
options.D: The order in which indexes were created

questions.answer_text: Statistics and estimated costs of candidate operations
questions.description: Optimizers estimate cardinalities and costs using statistics and choose a low-cost plan.

questions.question: Why do stale statistics matter?

options.A: They can cause inaccurate cardinality estimates and poor plan choices

questions.answer_text: They can cause inaccurate cardinality estimates and poor plan choices
questions.description: Optimizer statistics help estimate row counts and data distribution; stale stats can mislead plan selection.

questions.question: What is a sequential scan?

options.A: Reading table pages in storage order rather than locating rows through a selective index

questions.answer_text: Reading table pages in storage order rather than locating rows through a selective index
questions.description: A sequential scan reads the table’s pages in sequence and can be efficient for broad retrievals.

questions.question: What is an index-only scan?

options.A: Answering a query from index entries without fetching table rows where visibility/data permits
options.B: Scanning every index in the schema

questions.answer_text: Answering a query from index entries without fetching table rows where visibility/data permits
questions.description: An index-only scan avoids table lookups when all needed data is available and visibility conditions allow it.

questions.question: What is a bitmap index scan in systems that support it?

options.A: Combining index matches as bitmaps before fetching rows
options.C: A B-tree stored as an image

questions.answer_text: Combining index matches as bitmaps before fetching rows
questions.description: Bitmap scans can combine multiple predicates efficiently, especially when many rows match.

questions.question: What is a partial/filtered index?

options.A: An index containing only rows satisfying a predicate
options.B: An index storing half of each key
options.D: An index that stores no rows

questions.answer_text: An index containing only rows satisfying a predicate
questions.description: A partial index indexes only rows meeting its defining condition, reducing size for selected workloads.

questions.question: What is a unique index used to enforce?

options.A: Uniqueness of indexed key values

questions.answer_text: Uniqueness of indexed key values
questions.description: Unique indexes prevent duplicate indexed keys, with NULL semantics varying by engine.

questions.question: What is a foreign-key index recommendation about?

options.A: Indexing child FK columns can help joins/deletes/updates, but automatic creation varies
options.B: Every DBMS always creates it automatically
options.D: It changes the key into a primary key

questions.answer_text: Indexing child FK columns can help joins/deletes/updates, but automatic creation varies
questions.description: Many systems do not automatically index referencing columns; indexing may improve parent checks and joins.

questions.question: What does a range predicate like `created_at >= date1 AND created_at < date2` suit well?

options.A: An ordered index on created_at
options.D: A unique index on unrelated id

questions.answer_text: An ordered index on created_at
questions.description: B-tree indexes can support range scans over ordered values.

questions.question: What is a sargable predicate?

options.A: A predicate that can use an index search argument efficiently

questions.answer_text: A predicate that can use an index search argument efficiently
questions.description: Sargable conditions are structured so an index can efficiently locate qualifying rows.

questions.question: Why can `WHERE LOWER(name) = sam` fail to use a plain index on `name`?

options.A: The function is applied to the indexed column; an expression index or normalized value may be needed

questions.answer_text: The function is applied to the indexed column; an expression index or normalized value may be needed
questions.description: Applying a function to the column can prevent a direct seek on a plain index unless the optimizer has an expression index/transform.

questions.question: What is a common remedy for searching `name` case-insensitively with an index?

options.A: Use a suitable normalized/expression index or case-insensitive collation

questions.answer_text: Use a suitable normalized/expression index or case-insensitive collation
questions.description: The schema/index or collation should align with the comparison semantics used by the query.

questions.question: What is a range scan in a B-tree?

options.A: Traversing index entries between lower and upper key bounds
options.B: Reading every table in the database

questions.answer_text: Traversing index entries between lower and upper key bounds
questions.description: Ordered index entries make retrieval across a bounded key interval efficient.

questions.question: What is a database page/block?

options.A: A unit of storage transfer and buffering between disk and memory

questions.answer_text: A unit of storage transfer and buffering between disk and memory
questions.description: DBMSs read and write data in pages/blocks rather than individual bytes in most storage engines.

questions.question: What does a buffer pool/cache do?

options.A: Keeps database pages in memory to reduce storage I/O

questions.answer_text: Keeps database pages in memory to reduce storage I/O
questions.description: The buffer pool caches pages so repeated access can avoid physical storage reads.

questions.question: What is write-ahead logging (WAL) principle?

options.A: Log records reach durable storage before corresponding data pages are written
options.B: Data pages are written before any log

questions.answer_text: Log records reach durable storage before corresponding data pages are written
questions.description: WAL ensures recovery information is durable before modified data pages are persisted.

questions.question: Why may a transaction be aborted by the DBMS?

options.A: Deadlock, serialization conflict, constraint failure, or other error

questions.answer_text: Deadlock, serialization conflict, constraint failure, or other error
questions.description: Transactions can be rolled back due to concurrency control or constraint and runtime errors.

questions.question: What is a serialization anomaly?

options.A: A concurrent outcome not equivalent to any serial execution

questions.answer_text: A concurrent outcome not equivalent to any serial execution
questions.description: Serializable isolation aims to prevent executions whose effects cannot be explained by a serial order.

questions.question: What does snapshot isolation generally provide?

options.A: Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot, with conflict rules varying by DBMS
options.B: Every read sees the newest uncommitted value
options.C: It is identical to serializable in every implementation

questions.answer_text: Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot, with conflict rules varying by DBMS
questions.description: Snapshot isolation uses a consistent versioned view but may still permit anomalies unless stronger checks apply.

questions.question: What is lock escalation?

options.A: Replacing many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock
options.B: Turning a shared lock into an index

questions.answer_text: Replacing many fine-grained locks with a coarser lock
questions.description: Lock escalation reduces lock-management overhead by using a broader lock, with possible concurrency costs.

questions.question: What is a predicate/range lock used for in serializable execution?

options.A: Preventing conflicting inserts/updates into a queried range that could create phantoms

questions.answer_text: Preventing conflicting inserts/updates into a queried range that could create phantoms
questions.description: Range locking can protect the predicate against phantoms, though implementation varies.

questions.question: What is a lock timeout?

options.A: A maximum wait period before a lock request fails or is canceled
options.B: The time to build an index
options.D: The number of pages in a lock

questions.answer_text: A maximum wait period before a lock request fails or is canceled
questions.description: Lock timeouts bound how long a transaction waits for a conflicting lock.

questions.question: What does a transaction retry policy need to consider?

options.A: Retrying only safe/idempotent work and handling serialization/deadlock errors
options.B: Retry every error including syntax errors

questions.answer_text: Retrying only safe/idempotent work and handling serialization/deadlock errors
questions.description: Transient concurrency errors can be retried, but application side effects and idempotency must be handled carefully.

questions.question: What is an index page split?

options.A: A B-tree node is divided when there is insufficient room for an insertion
options.B: A transaction is split into two commits

questions.answer_text: A B-tree node is divided when there is insufficient room for an insertion
questions.description: Page splits preserve the tree structure as ordered index entries are inserted.

questions.question: What can excessive page splits contribute to?

options.A: Fragmentation and write overhead

questions.answer_text: Fragmentation and write overhead
questions.description: Frequent splits can increase write work and affect page layout, depending on workload and engine.

questions.question: What is an index fill factor?

options.A: A setting/target for how full index pages are populated
options.B: The number of columns in a key

questions.answer_text: A setting/target for how full index pages are populated
questions.description: Fill factor leaves free space in pages to accommodate future inserts/updates in some DBMSs.

questions.question: What does a descending index key order help with?

options.A: Some descending order/range query plans, depending on DBMS and index definition

questions.answer_text: Some descending order/range query plans, depending on DBMS and index definition
questions.description: Index key ordering can align with ORDER BY and range requirements, subject to optimizer support.

questions.question: What is index fragmentation?

options.A: Suboptimal physical/logical page organization that can increase I/O

questions.answer_text: Suboptimal physical/logical page organization that can increase I/O
questions.description: Fragmentation may reduce locality and increase reads, though its impact depends on workload and engine.

questions.question: What does an optimizer cardinality estimate represent?

options.A: Estimated number of rows produced by an operation
options.B: The number of columns in the database

questions.answer_text: Estimated number of rows produced by an operation
questions.description: Cardinality estimates predict row counts at plan nodes and influence join/order choices.

questions.question: What is a nested-loop join often good for?

options.A: Small outer input with an indexed lookup into the inner input
options.B: Only two huge unsorted tables with no index

questions.answer_text: Small outer input with an indexed lookup into the inner input
questions.description: Nested loops can be efficient when the outer side is small and inner lookup is indexed.

questions.question: What is a hash join often suited for?

options.A: Large equality joins when inputs can be hashed
options.B: Range joins on ordered values only

questions.answer_text: Large equality joins when inputs can be hashed
questions.description: Hash joins build a hash structure on one input and probe it with the other for equality matches.

questions.question: What is a merge join often suited for?

options.A: Inputs ordered on join keys
options.B: Any two tables without reading them

questions.answer_text: Inputs ordered on join keys
questions.description: Merge joins advance through ordered inputs and can be efficient when keys are already sorted/indexed.

questions.question: Does SQL text join order necessarily dictate physical join order?

options.A: No; the optimizer may reorder joins when semantics permit

questions.answer_text: No; the optimizer may reorder joins when semantics permit
questions.description: Cost-based optimizers can choose a different physical join order while preserving query semantics.

questions.question: What does partition pruning do?

options.A: Skips partitions that cannot satisfy a query predicate

questions.answer_text: Skips partitions that cannot satisfy a query predicate
questions.description: Partition pruning avoids scanning partitions excluded by partition-key predicates.

questions.question: What is table partitioning primarily for?

options.A: Dividing a large table into manageable physical/logical pieces by a key or rule

questions.answer_text: Dividing a large table into manageable physical/logical pieces by a key or rule
questions.description: Partitioning can improve manageability and some access patterns when queries align with partitioning.

questions.question: What is a common partitioning pitfall?

options.A: Queries that do not filter on partition keys may still scan many/all partitions

questions.answer_text: Queries that do not filter on partition keys may still scan many/all partitions
questions.description: Partitioning benefits depend on pruning, balance, and workload; it is not automatically faster.

questions.question: What is a primary-key index commonly used for?

options.A: Fast key lookup and enforcement of uniqueness

questions.answer_text: Fast key lookup and enforcement of uniqueness
questions.description: DBMSs typically create or use an index structure to enforce primary-key uniqueness efficiently.

questions.question: What is a bitmap index typically useful for?

options.A: Low-cardinality columns in some analytic workloads
options.B: High-write transactional tables in every DBMS

questions.answer_text: Low-cardinality columns in some analytic workloads
questions.description: Bitmap indexes can be efficient for low-cardinality predicates and analytic combinations, but write behavior varies.

questions.question: What is a full-text index designed for?

options.A: Tokenized text search and relevance-like matching

questions.answer_text: Tokenized text search and relevance-like matching
questions.description: Full-text indexes support linguistic/token search beyond ordinary equality or prefix lookups.

questions.question: What is a spatial index designed for?

options.A: Geometric/location predicates

questions.answer_text: Geometric/location predicates
questions.description: Spatial indexes accelerate spatial relationships such as containment or proximity, using specialized structures.

questions.question: What does an index seek generally indicate?

options.A: Navigating to a key range or value in an index

questions.answer_text: Navigating to a key range or value in an index
questions.description: An index seek uses key predicates to locate a subset of index entries.

questions.question: What does an index scan generally indicate?

options.A: Reading a substantial portion or all of an index
options.B: A table always returns one row
options.D: A query has no WHERE clause

questions.answer_text: Reading a substantial portion or all of an index
questions.description: An index scan walks index entries and may be chosen when it is cheaper or provides needed ordering.

questions.question: Why is `SELECT *` sometimes harmful for a high-volume endpoint?

options.A: It may fetch unnecessary columns and prevent a narrow covering access path

questions.answer_text: It may fetch unnecessary columns and prevent a narrow covering access path
questions.description: Selecting only needed columns can reduce I/O/network payload and may permit covering-index plans.

questions.question: What is an execution plan regression?

options.A: A query begins using a slower plan after changes to data, stats, schema, or software

questions.answer_text: A query begins using a slower plan after changes to data, stats, schema, or software
questions.description: Plan changes and estimation errors can make an otherwise unchanged query slower.

questions.question: What is a covering composite index advantage?

options.A: It may satisfy filtering and projection from the index without base-row lookups

questions.answer_text: It may satisfy filtering and projection from the index without base-row lookups
questions.description: When all needed columns are present, a covering index may reduce heap/table access.

questions.question: Why should indexes on frequently updated columns be considered carefully?

options.A: Updates may require index maintenance and page changes
options.D: They force all scans to be sequential

questions.answer_text: Updates may require index maintenance and page changes
questions.description: Changing an indexed key can require removing and inserting index entries.

questions.question: What does an index predicate on a leading key support most naturally?

options.A: A seek or range scan using that key
options.B: A lookup on an unrelated trailing column always

questions.answer_text: A seek or range scan using that key
questions.description: The first key column provides the strongest direct access path for a conventional composite B-tree.

questions.question: What is a histogram statistic used for?

options.A: Estimating data distribution and predicate selectivity

questions.answer_text: Estimating data distribution and predicate selectivity
questions.description: Histograms summarize value distributions to improve optimizer selectivity estimates.

questions.question: What does parameter sniffing/plan sensitivity refer to in some DBMSs?

options.A: A cached plan based on parameter values may perform poorly for different values
options.B: A database password is read from SQL
options.C: A parameter is always interpolated unsafely

questions.answer_text: A cached plan based on parameter values may perform poorly for different values
questions.description: Some optimizers compile/cache plans using observed parameter values, and data skew can make one plan unsuitable for other inputs.

questions.question: What is a query hint?

options.A: An instruction or suggestion to influence optimizer behavior, vendor-specific

questions.answer_text: An instruction or suggestion to influence optimizer behavior, vendor-specific
questions.description: Hints can affect plan choice but are dialect-specific and may reduce portability.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `ANALYZE`/statistics collection in many DBMSs?

options.A: Refresh optimizer statistics from table data

questions.answer_text: Refresh optimizer statistics from table data
questions.description: Statistics collection updates estimates used by the query optimizer.

questions.question: What does vacuum/garbage collection in an MVCC database often help with?

options.A: Reclaiming or reusing obsolete row versions and maintaining visibility metadata

questions.answer_text: Reclaiming or reusing obsolete row versions and maintaining visibility metadata
questions.description: MVCC engines need cleanup of obsolete versions to control storage and maintain performance.

questions.question: What is a hot row contention problem?

options.A: Many transactions concurrently update the same row or small set of rows
options.B: A table has too many columns
options.C: A query uses a cold cache

questions.answer_text: Many transactions concurrently update the same row or small set of rows
questions.description: Contending updates on a small number of rows serialize and can limit throughput.

questions.question: What is a common benefit of batching inserts?

options.A: Lower per-statement/network overhead and improved throughput
options.D: Every row receives a unique index

questions.answer_text: Lower per-statement/network overhead and improved throughput
questions.description: Batching amortizes round trips and statement setup, though batch size and transaction scope require care.

questions.question: What is the risk of an excessively large transaction?

options.A: Long lock duration, larger rollback/recovery work, and resource pressure

questions.answer_text: Long lock duration, larger rollback/recovery work, and resource pressure
questions.description: Very large transactions can hold locks longer and increase log, memory, and rollback costs.

questions.question: What does a read replica commonly serve?

options.A: Read traffic or reporting, subject to replication lag
options.B: Primary writes only in every architecture

questions.answer_text: Read traffic or reporting, subject to replication lag
questions.description: Replicas can scale read workloads, but asynchronous replication may make them stale.

questions.question: What is replication lag?

options.A: Delay between a primary change and its visibility on a replica
options.B: The time to build an index

questions.answer_text: Delay between a primary change and its visibility on a replica
questions.description: Replica data may trail the primary due to asynchronous log shipping or apply delays.

questions.question: What is a write-ahead log checkpoint?

options.A: A recovery point that helps bound redo work by flushing/synchronizing state

questions.answer_text: A recovery point that helps bound redo work by flushing/synchronizing state
questions.description: Checkpoints record recovery progress and help limit work needed during crash recovery.

questions.question: What does a clustered storage choice make important for a table’s key?

options.A: The key/order can influence row placement and range locality

questions.answer_text: The key/order can influence row placement and range locality
questions.description: When row storage follows an index key, key selection can affect locality and page splits.

questions.question: What should be verified before adding an index to address a slow query?

options.A: The actual plan, selectivity, write cost, and workload
options.D: Whether the table has a primary key

questions.answer_text: The actual plan, selectivity, write cost, and workload
questions.description: Index choices should follow plan evidence and workload trade-offs rather than guesswork.
